title: Faster Vision Transformers with Adaptive Patches
claim: Uniform fixed-size patching wastes tokens on homogeneous regions; content-aware patch sizes use fewer tokens while keeping detail where it matters.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, same image with different patch grid overlays
description: A wide strip of three panels showing the same photograph of an orange-and-black oriole perched on a diagonal mossy branch against a blurred green background. The left panel is the plain original image. The middle panel, labeled Standard Vision Transformer, overlays a dense uniform white grid of small square patches across the whole image. The right panel, labeled Adaptive Patch Transformer (Ours), overlays a quadtree-style grid. Large patches cover the blurry, homogeneous background, and small patches concentrate on the bird, its beak, the branch edges and the tail. The eye goes first to the bird, then to the contrast between the uniform grid and the variable-size grid. Captions are plain serif text under each panel. There are no arrows or other annotations.
caption: Adaptive Patch Sizing. We present APT, Adaptive Patch Transformers, which significantly accelerate vision transformer training and inference by patchifying images based on their content. Complex regions receive more, smaller tokens, while simpler, homogeneous regions receive fewer.
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) partition input images into uniformly sized patches regardless of their content, resulting in long input sequence lengths for high-resolution images. We present Adaptive Patch Transformers (APT), which addresses this by using multiple different patch sizes within the same image. APT reduces the total number of input tokens by allocating larger patch sizes in more homogeneous areas and smaller patches in more complex ones. APT achieves a drastic speedup in ViT inference and training, increasing throughput by 40\% on ViT-L and 50\% on ViT-H while maintaining downstream performance. It can be applied to a previously fine-tuned ViT and converges in as little as 1 epoch. It also significantly reduces training and inference time without loss of performance in high-resolution dense visual tasks, achieving up to 30\% faster training and inference in visual QA, object detection, and semantic segmentation. We will release all code and trained models.
